newsitem.title: JAPAN: Albright holds talks with Japan foreign minister.
newsitem.headline: Albright holds talks with Japan foreign minister.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright arrived in Tokyo on Sunday, briefly taking a break from heavyweight diplomacy to confirm strong ties with its key ally in Asia.

"The relationship between the United States and Japan within the last 50 years can be noted as one of the exemplary post-World War Two relations that has evolved into a full-scope relationship," Albright said ahead of a meeting with Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters the two ministers would touch on a wide range of topics such as Asia-Pacific security including China and North Korea, the Peru hostage crisis, Burma, United Nations reform and the Bosnian situation.
"She's very keen to make sure she is active on all issues," Burns told reporters.
Albright arrived from Seoul as part of a nine-nation tour, her first overseas visit since becoming secretary of state last month.

Her visit coincides with leadership turmoil in North Korea, the unpredictable Stalinist state which is one of the main strategic reasons for a large American military presence in Japan, particularly on the southern island of Okinawa.
Some Okinawa residents have started a campaign to shut the bases because of worries about the impact U.S. servicemen have on the local community.
"The U.S.-Japan relationship is important not only for the two nations but for the international community, particularly for the Asia-Pacific region," Ikeda said in his welcoming speech to Albright.
Aside from confirmation of U.S.-Japan security ties, the two ministers will likely touch on the thorny issue of the U.S. military presence in Okinawa.

Ikeda, who visited Okinawa this week ahead of Albright's trip, is expected to bring up an incident in which U.S. Marine Corps jets inadvertently fired bullets containing depleted uranium near an island off Okinawa.

The future of the U.S. bases on Okinawa has been threatened, just as tensions rise on the Korean peninsula, by the refusal of about 3,000 landowners to approve an extension of leases on the land occupied by the installations.
About 49,000 U.S. military personnel are based in Japan, more than half of them on the sub-tropical island 1,600 km (1,000 miles) southwest of Tokyo.
Okinawa hosts more than 75 percent of all U.S. military bases and Okinawans have long complained of noise, accidents and crime in areas near the sprawling military facilities.
Albright has indicated that Japan is the key to ensuring stability in Asia and is expected to urge Tokyo to find a peaceful way out of its row with Okinawan residents.
"We admire particularly what has been going on in Japan as the key to our security in the Asian region," Albright said.

Albright will also hold brief talks with trade minister Shinji Sato and defense chief Fumio Kyuma on Sunday and meet Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto over breakfast on Monday before leaving for Beijing.
